milestones.title: Sun Quan walls Xiakou on Snake Hill
milestones.detail: The Wu ruler Sun Quan built the walled town of Xiakou on Snake Hill in today's Wuchang, with a watchtower that became the Yellow Crane Tower. A slightly earlier fort, Queyue, had been built across the river in Hanyang at the end of the Han.

milestones.title: Wuying Pagoda built as Mongol armies close in
milestones.detail: The Wuying Pagoda in Wuchang was first built in 1270, at the end of the Song dynasty, between Mongol attacks on the town (Kublai Khan had besieged it in 1259).

milestones.title: Wuchang becomes capital of Huguang province
milestones.detail: Under the Yuan dynasty Wuchang was made the seat of the Huguang provincial government, beginning its long role as the administrative centre of central China.

milestones.title: Han River shifts course; Hankou emerges
milestones.detail: During the Chenghua reign (1465-1487) the Han River moved its mouth to the north side of Turtle Hill, cutting a new bank off from Hanyang. The sheltered river mouth quickly grew into the market town of Hankou.
milestones.source: Kangxi-era Hanyang fu zhi, juan 1, via https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/汉口

milestones.title: Hankou opened as a treaty port
milestones.detail: Under the Treaty of Tianjin and the Convention of Peking, Hankou was opened to foreign trade in 1861 and a British concession was laid out along the Yangtze. French, Russian, German and Japanese concessions followed by 1898.

milestones.title: Zhang Zhidong begins industrialising the towns
milestones.detail: Zhang Zhidong became Viceroy of Huguang in 1889 and over 18 years founded the Hanyang ironworks, the Hanyang (Hubei) Arsenal, textile mills and modern schools.

milestones.title: Beijing-Hankou railway completed
milestones.detail: The Jinghan railway, built between 1897 and 1906, linked Hankou to Beijing and made the towns a transfer point between rail and river traffic.

milestones.title: Wuchang Uprising; Hankou burned
milestones.detail: The uprising of 10 October 1911 in Wuchang set off the revolution that ended the Qing dynasty. In the fighting that followed, a fire burned for three days and destroyed much of Hankou.

milestones.title: Three towns merged as Wuhan, Nationalist capital
milestones.detail: On 1 January 1927 the Nationalist government, newly moved from Guangzhou, combined Wuchang, Hankou and Hanyang into a single city named Wuhan. The towns were separated again in 1929 and reunited for good in 1949.

milestones.title: Yangtze flood submerges the city
milestones.detail: In the 1931 China floods about 32 square miles of the city lay under water for close to three months.

milestones.title: Battle of Wuhan and Japanese occupation
milestones.detail: Wuhan served as China's provisional capital after the fall of Nanjing. After a battle lasting from June to 27 October 1938 the city was taken by Japanese forces.

milestones.title: US firebombing of Hankou
milestones.detail: On 18 December 1944 American bombers attacked the Japanese-held city; Hankou's 1946 statistics counted more than 20,000 killed or injured in the December raids.

milestones.title: PLA enters; Wuhan permanently unified
milestones.detail: People's Liberation Army troops entered the city on 16 May 1949, and Hankou, Wuchang and the urban part of Hanyang were merged into the single municipality of Wuhan.

milestones.title: First Yangtze River Bridge opens
milestones.detail: The 1,670 m road-and-rail Wuhan Yangtze River Bridge opened on 15 October 1957, joining Wuchang to Hanyang and the Beijing-Hankou railway to the line to Guangzhou.

milestones.title: Wuhan Metro Line 1 opens
milestones.detail: Line 1 opened on 28 July 2004, making Wuhan the seventh city in mainland China with rapid transit.

milestones.title: COVID-19 lockdown
milestones.detail: The city where SARS-CoV-2 was first identified was locked down in January 2020; the lockdown ended on 8 April 2020.

landmarks.name: Hongshan Pagoda (Baotong Temple)
landmarks.note: Built 1280-1291. Coordinates are those of Baotong Temple; the pagoda stands on the hillside just behind it.

landmarks.name: Jianghan Customs House (Hankow Customs House)
landmarks.source: https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/江汉关大楼 ; coordinates from OpenStreetMap
landmarks.note: Completed 21 January 1924; the tallest building in Wuhan at the time. Chinese Wikipedia gives 45.85 m for the building and 23.1 m for the clock-tower section.

landmarks.name: Yellow Crane Tower (1985 reconstruction)
landmarks.note: A tower has stood on Snake Hill in various forms since 223; the last on the original site was built in 1868 and destroyed in 1884. The present concrete tower stands about 1 km from that site.

landmarks.name: Tortoise Mountain TV Tower
landmarks.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tortoise_Mountain_TV_Tower ; completion year from https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/龟山电视塔
landmarks.note: Height to antenna tip as given by Wikipedia; observation deck at 221.2 m.

notes: Start date: Wuhan is the 20th-century merger of Wuchang, Hankou and Hanyang, so the start is the earliest securely dated walled town among them: Xiakou, built by Sun Quan on Snake Hill (Wuchang) in 223 CE, which both English and Chinese Wikipedia treat as the foundation of the city. Two earlier candidates were not used: Queyue fort in Hanyang, built at the very end of the Han (English Wikipedia says 206, uncited; Chinese Wikipedia calls it the earliest known town site in the urban area but gives no year), and the Shang-period walled site of Panlongcheng (c. 1500 BCE) in Huangpi District, which is in the municipality but is not continuous with the later towns. The often-quoted '3,500 years of history' rests on Panlongcheng. Hankou itself only dates from the Han River's change of course in the Chenghua reign (1465-1487); 1465 in the milestones stands for that reign, not an exact year. Population: thin and uneven. Chandler's (1987) row, as digitised by Reba, Reitsma & Seto (2016), is labelled 'Wuhan' with the alternative name 'Wuchang'; its figures up to 1875 are far too small to include Hankou and are treated here as Wuchang alone, while those from 1900 are for the three towns. That reading is our inference from the labels and magnitudes, not something the dataset states. As a result the series before 1900 omits Hankou, which by the early 18th century was one of China's four great trading towns; no sourced Hankou-only or Hanyang-only figure was found, so the pre-1900 curve understates the conurbation. There is no figure between 223 and 750 or between 800 and 1200 (Chandler's intermediate years 800, 1250, 1259, 1350, 1450, 1550, 1575, 1650 and 1825 were dropped). The 1936 and 1940 figures come from Chinese Wikipedia's citations of the Wuhan gazetteer and of Pi Mingxiu's histories and could not be checked at source (the archived gazetteer page was unreachable). Chinese Wikipedia also quotes the 1923 China Year Book (Hankou 850,000, Wuchang city 250,000) and says the three towns passed 1,000,000 in 1930; these are not in the series because they could not be traced further. No census figure before 1950 was located. Landmarks: the Wuhan Yangtze River Bridge (1957), Guiyuan Temple, the Wuying Pagoda (1270) and the 1911 uprising memorial were left out for lack of a sourced height; the 9.36 m Yuan-dynasty Shengxiang stupa by the Yellow Crane Tower was left out for lack of a sourced date. Modern tower heights, years and coordinates are from the CTBUH Skyscraper Center city listing for Wuhan (WGS-84; Greenland Center checked against OpenStreetMap). CTBUH lists Wuhan Center as 'Wuhan Tower', 443.13 m.
